opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really fair question, and honestly I go back and forth on it myself.

If you look at almost any single task in isolation, a humanoid is rarely the most efficient solution. A robotic arm on a rail will beat it in a factory. A wheeled base with a gripper is cheaper and more stable in a warehouse. A dishwasher is better at washing dishes than any humanoid will be for a long time. So if the question is "what's the best tool for this one job," the answer is almost never a humanoid.

But I think that framing misses why people are excited. The world we've built is shaped around the human body: stairs, door handles, tools, kitchens, car seats, shelves at certain heights. A humanoid's real value proposition isn't being optimal at one task. It's being *good enough* at a very wide range of tasks without redesigning the environment. That's the same bet we made with general-purpose computers over specialized machines.

There's also a data argument that I find compelling. We have an enormous amount of human video and demonstration data. If your robot has roughly the same body plan as a person, the gap between "watching a human do something" and "doing it yourself" gets smaller. That matters a lot when learning, not hand-engineering, is the main way these systems improve.

Now, the limitations are real, and I don't want to downplay them. Hands are still very far from human dexterity. Tactile sensing is primitive. Battery life is short. Reliability is nowhere near what you'd need for someone's home, where a failure isn't a lost part, it's a broken object or someone getting hurt. And cost is still far too high for most applications to make economic sense.

So my honest view is that the near term will be dominated by simpler, specialized form factors, and that's healthy. Humanoids will probably first prove themselves in semi-structured settings, like logistics and certain manufacturing lines, where tasks vary but conditions are controlled. The home is a much longer horizon.

Long term, though, I'm optimistic. I don't think the humanoid has to win every task. It just has to become the default platform for the long tail of tasks that nobody will ever build a dedicated machine for. And that long tail is most of life.

r001.rationale: It says humanoid robots’ cost is too high, but does not attribute that cost to immature hardware technology.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning and real limitations, but does not say their lack of intelligence is due to immature software technology.

r003.rationale: It says simpler, specialized form factors will dominate in the near term while humanoids may serve a broad long tail of tasks, giving both substantial roles.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that humanoids are a bet on generality, and right now generality is expensive and immature. If you look at any single task in a warehouse or a factory, a purpose-built machine almost always wins today. A wheeled base with an arm is cheaper, more reliable, and easier to certify than a bipedal robot that has to balance just to stand still. So if your question is "what should I deploy next quarter," the humanoid is rarely the answer.

But I'd separate the near-term economics from the long-term thesis. The reason people are excited about humanoids isn't that legs are a great engineering choice. It's that the entire built world was designed around the human body. Door handles, stairs, shelves, tools, vehicles. If you can make one platform that operates in that environment without retrofitting it, the addressable market stops being "this one warehouse" and becomes "everywhere humans work." That's a very different kind of bet, and it's why so much capital is flowing in despite the current demos being, frankly, underwhelming when you watch them closely.

The real gating factor isn't the hardware anymore. Actuators, batteries, and sensors have gotten good enough that you can build a reasonable body. The gate is the brain. We don't yet have robot foundation models that generalize across tasks the way language models generalize across text. Data is the bottleneck. You can't scrape the internet for manipulation experience the way you can for words. So what we're seeing is a lot of teleoperation, simulation, and very narrow learned skills stitched together.

My view is that the humanoid form factor will make sense once the software catches up, and simpler tools will dominate until then. The companies that survive will be the ones who find a narrow commercial wedge now, something boring like tote handling or machine tending, and use that revenue and data to fund the general capability. The ones that go straight for the sci-fi vision without an intermediate business will mostly run out of money before the technology arrives.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware has gotten good enough and identifies the brain and data as the main bottlenecks. It does not attribute current high costs to immature hardware.

r002.rationale: It says the brain is the gate, that robot foundation models do not yet generalize, and that humanoids will make sense once software catches up.

r003.rationale: It says simpler tools will dominate until software improves, but does not clearly state that simpler tools and humanoids will both have substantial roles.

astra-6.text:
I think the long-term potential is huge, but we have to be honest about what they can do today. If you want to move a box from one place to another, you probably don’t need a humanoid robot. A conveyor belt or a robot on wheels might do that more cheaply and reliably.

The interesting question is whether one robot can do many different tasks in an environment built for people. We have stairs, doors, shelves, tools—all designed around the human body. A humanoid could potentially work in that environment without us redesigning everything. But that advantage only matters if it can actually perform the work reliably and at a reasonable cost.

So I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t assume that looking human makes a robot useful. I’d start with a specific job where it solves a real problem, then expand its capabilities. The prospect is exciting because of that potential flexibility, but there’s still a big gap between an impressive demonstration and something you can depend on every day.

r001.rationale: The response mentions cost as a factor in choosing simpler tools, but does not attribute humanoid robots’ high cost to immature hardware.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and capability limits but does not describe a lack of intelligence or attribute it to immature software.

r003.rationale: It contrasts humanoids with conveyor belts and wheeled robots, but does not state that humanoids and simpler tools such as hammers can coexist with substantial roles for both.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic about humanoid robots in the long term, but I think we have to be practical about where they’re useful today. If a task can be done reliably and cheaply with a simpler machine, why use a humanoid? The goal should be to solve the problem, not to make the robot look like us.

The interesting opportunity is that so much of our world is designed for people—our tools, our buildings, our workspaces. A robot that can operate in those environments and handle different tasks could be very valuable. But that flexibility has to translate into real reliability and a reasonable cost. I think progress will come from finding specific tasks where that capability matters, proving it works, and expanding from there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses requiring a reasonable cost, but does not attribute humanoid robots’ high cost to immature hardware technology.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention current lack of intelligence or attribute it to immature software.

r003.rationale: It says simpler machines suit tasks they handle reliably and cheaply, and humanoids may help in human-designed environments. It does not clearly state that both will coexist with substantial roles.
